The day length is then that angle divided by 7.5, which is 14.844 hours, or 14 hours 51 minutes. The same latitude in the southern hemisphere gives an hour angle of 68.672 degrees and 9.155 hours, and the two figures sum to exactly 24 because the two latitudes are mirror images and the declination has one sign. Two checks are worth making. At the equator the product of the tangents is zero whatever the declination, so the hour angle is 90 degrees and the day length is 12 hours everywhere on the equinox. And the day length reaches 24 hours only where the latitude and the declination add to 90, which on this date is 66.56 degrees north.

questions.explanation: The subsolar point sits where the sun's rays strike vertically, which is directly below the point on the globe where the sun's declination places it, so the two are the same latitude. On the December solstice the sun stands over 23.44 degrees south, and six months earlier it stood over 23.44 degrees north, because the axis of rotation is tilted 23.44 degrees from the plane of the orbit and points the same way all year: what changes is which hemisphere the tilt is leaning towards. That is why the two solstice declinations are equal and opposite and why no point on the globe ever sees the sun directly overhead at a latitude beyond 23.44 degrees in either hemisphere. The consequence for day length is the mirror relationship, since the northern and southern day lengths on any given date always add to 24 hours.

questions.explanation: A quarter of 1,361 is 340.25 watts per square metre, and the figure can be checked rather than remembered. Integrating the daily mean over latitude, weighted by the area element cos of latitude, and over the year's declinations gives 421.24 at the equator, 368.36 at 30 degrees, 229.65 at 60 degrees and 137.27 at the pole, and the area-weighted integral of those values returns the global mean. A second, purely geometric route gives the same answer: at any point on the globe the sun is above the horizon for part of each rotation, and the mean of the positive part of the cosine of the zenith angle over a full year is exactly one quarter, so the factor of four has nothing to do with the tilt of the axis. The consequence is that the poles receive more annual energy than their latitude suggests, because a polar summer of continuous daylight offsets a polar winter of none, and it is the seasonal range rather than the annual mean that is extreme.

questions.explanation: A point is in polar day when the sun's declination and the point's latitude are of the same sign and their sum exceeds 90 degrees, because that is the condition under which the sun's daily path never crosses the horizon. The threshold is therefore latitude 66.56 degrees, which is 90 minus the obliquity, and the whole polar day belt narrows to nothing at the equinoxes when the declination is zero. The fact that one hemisphere can be in continuous daylight while the other is in continuous dark is the clearest demonstration that the axis keeps a fixed direction and the orbit changes the hemisphere the tilt leans towards.

questions.explanation: The fourth power is the whole point of the calculation. Raising the temperature from 288 to 300 kelvin multiplies the outgoing radiation by (300/288) to the fourth, which is 1.178, so 390.1 becomes 459.3 watts per square metre, a rise of 69.2. A temperature change of 4% has produced a radiation change of 18%, and that convexity is what makes surface temperature a sensitive control on the energy budget. It is also why the same argument runs in reverse at the top of the atmosphere, where a warmer atmosphere emits more longwave radiation to space and so must receive more to stay in balance, which is the mechanism behind the greenhouse effect. The wavelength claim in the third option is true and irrelevant: the peak of the curve shifts to a shorter wavelength, but the total energy emitted over all wavelengths rises.

questions.explanation: A Bowen ratio of 0.3 says the sensible heat is 0.3 of the latent heat, so if the latent heat is L the sensible heat is 0.3L and the pair together is 1.3L. Setting 1.3L to 100 gives L = 76.9 and a sensible heat of 23.1 watts per square metre, and the two sum back to 100 as a check. The dividing by 1.3 is the step that is usually skipped, and skipping it is what produces the 30 and 70 in the first distractor. The ratio is a compact index of how a surface spends its available energy, and a low value in a hot dry month means the surface is dry and the available energy is going into warming the air, while a high value means the surface is wet and most of the energy is being used to evaporate water. A negative ratio is possible and is a further diagnostic, since it means the surface is losing heat by evaporation faster than it gains it, which points to a supply of water from below.

answer.exemplar: Potential evapotranspiration is the evaporation that would occur from a surface of the same area covered with water and with the net radiation available, sometimes described as the reference figure. It is computable from a temperature, a wind speed, a humidity and a radiation, which is exactly why it is useful: it can be estimated for every day of a record without a measurement of the soil or the vegetation. Actual evapotranspiration is what the surface really evaporates, and it falls short whenever the supply of water is the limiting factor rather than the supply of energy. Over a wet month in a temperate climate the two are nearly the same, and over a dry month the ratio falls well below one, and the shortfall is a direct measure of the water the vegetation could not get. The reason the ratio is the useful figure is that it separates the two things that can limit a catchment's water yield. A low ratio in a month with a large potential figure means water is short, and the response belongs in soil water storage and in the choice of crop. A low ratio in a cool month means the atmosphere itself is demanding little, and the catchment may be losing water to a lack of demand rather than to a lack of supply, which points to storage and to the timing of irrigation instead. Reporting the two numbers separately invites the reader to treat every shortfall as a drought; reporting the ratio makes the reason for it visible.

questions.explanation: The question asks for a distinction and then for a recommendation about reporting, and the recommendation turns on what the ratio removes. The ratio divides a measured quantity by a computed one, so it strips out the demand of the atmosphere and leaves only the degree to which supply limited it, which is the part a manager can act on. Reporting the two figures separately leaves the reader to do that division and, more importantly, leaves room to read every shortfall as a drought.
questions.hint: Ask what limits evaporation in each case: the energy available, or the water available.

questions.explanation: The balance is between two forces, the pressure-gradient force pushing across the isobars and the Coriolis force pushing across the direction of travel. If the wind crossed the isobars at a right angle, the Coriolis force would act along the gradient and the two could not balance, because neither is opposing the other. The only geometry in which they oppose is one where the Coriolis force points back up the gradient, which means the wind lies along the isobars. Which side the low pressure falls on then follows from the sense of the Coriolis deflection, which is to the right of the direction of travel in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern, so the low pressure is on the left of the flow in the north and on the right in the south. The surface wind departs from this because friction weakens the Coriolis force and leaves a residual component down the gradient, which is why surface winds cross the isobars towards the low.
questions.hint: Ask which direction each of the two balancing forces actually points.

answer.exemplar: The drift is the product of the Coriolis parameter, the sine of the latitude, the speed of the parcel and the square of the elapsed time, and each factor is doing work. Doubling the time quadruples the drift, because the parcel is being turned continuously rather than launched on a curve, so the accumulated displacement is quadratic in time while the distance travelled is linear. That is the reason a constant deflection angle is the wrong model: with the angle the parcel's velocity is turned by a fixed amount every second, and the resulting path is a circle, whereas the Coriolis acceleration depends on the velocity itself and the path curves at a rate set by how fast the parcel is moving. The acceleration is proportional to the speed and to the sine of the latitude, so halving the speed halves the drift and the drift vanishes at the equator, where the Coriolis parameter is zero. The figure works out at 66,826 metres, or 66825.7 km, after one hour at 100 metres per second, which is the same as a constant angle of 20.4 degrees over the whole hour, and the two agree because the two formulations are equivalent: the deflection angle satisfies the tangent of the angle equal to the parameter times the sine of latitude times the time, and the displacement is half the velocity times the time times that tangent. The same relation is why a projectile can be deflected by hundreds of metres over a long flight, and why the deflection of a freely moving object is negligible over a short one.

questions.explanation: The calculation has to be done as an acceleration integrated over time, and the reason the drift is quadratic in time is that the acceleration depends on the velocity, which is itself changing direction. A constant deflection angle describes a different physical situation, one in which the turn is imposed at a fixed rate regardless of speed, and the numerical agreement between the two routes holds only for the special case of a constant speed in a constant Coriolis field.
questions.hint: The drift grows with the square of the time, so work the acceleration out and integrate it.

questions.explanation: The Coriolis parameter is proportional to the sine of the latitude, so it is positive in the northern hemisphere and negative in the southern, and a balance that involves dividing by it reverses the direction of the resulting wind. Both are the same sense for a low, and both reverse for a high, and the term that describes them is the same in the two hemispheres for exactly this reason. A student who expects a hemisphere to have a fixed sense of rotation is remembering the shape of the globe rather than the sign of the parameter, and the bearings settle it.

questions.explanation: The high pressure belt is the descending limb of the Hadley cell. Air that rose at the equator, lost moisture and turned poleward aloft reaches about 30 degrees where it sinks, and a subsiding column is compressed as well as warmed, so the pressure at the surface rises. The descending air then spreads away from the belt in both directions, and the equatorward branch is the trade wind. Computing the geostrophic wind in that branch confirms the direction: with pressure rising towards the north at 15 degrees north the wind blows towards a bearing of 270 degrees, that is from the east, and at 15 degrees south the same argument gives a bearing of 90 degrees, that is from the east in the other hemisphere. Those are the trades, and their reliability is the reason shipping used them before engines and the reason they are the world's most persistent wind belt.

questions.explanation: The rainfall sits at the equator, and the mechanism is ascent followed by cooling. Air rises in the equatorial branch of both cells, and rising air expands as the pressure falls on it, so it cools adiabatically; when its dew point is reached water condenses and the latent heat released makes the ascent warmer and faster, which is what keeps the branch going. The poleward return flow aloft is therefore comparatively dry, and the descending branch at 30 degrees warms on the way down, which suppresses cloud. The single Hadley cell cannot be the whole story of the planet's rainfall, which is why the cell is described as a simplified picture: the mid-latitude storms and the polar cell account for a large share of the rain, and the dry subtropics exist because the descending branch is warmer and drier at the surface than the air rising at the equator.

questions.explanation: The naming of an air mass carries three pieces of information, and the reading has to use all of them. Maritime or continental says where the mass spent its time over water or over land, which sets its moisture and its temperature contrast; tropical or polar says the latitude of its source region; and the direction from which it arrives is the last word in the name. A maritime tropical mass is warm and wet, a maritime polar mass is cool and wet, and a continental polar mass is cold and dry. The fronts that matter form between masses of contrasting temperature, so a maritime tropical air meeting a maritime polar air gives a front, and the same tropical air meeting a cold continental polar air gives a sharper and faster-moving one. The sequence of fronts that then passes through a region is what a weather map is really describing, and the mass behind each front is what the following weather will be.

questions.explanation: The sea breeze is a direct consequence of the difference in heat capacity between water and land. Water warms and cools far more slowly, so on a sunny day the land surface becomes warmer than the air over the sea, the air over the land rises, and the air it draws in from the sea is the sea breeze; at night the land cools faster than the water, the circulation reverses, and the land breeze carries the accumulated pollutants away from the coast. The timing is what makes the sea breeze contentious. The deepest mixing and the strongest inflow usually occur in the middle of the afternoon, when the temperature contrast is greatest, and they collapse within an hour or two of sunset. Any dispersion modelling that assumes a steady on-shore flow through the evening will therefore overestimate the transport and underestimate the concentrations in the streets nearest the coast, because the flow that has been diluting the plume all day reverses and starts trapping it.

questions.explanation: An inversion is a stable layer, and stability is exactly the property that suppresses vertical mixing, because any parcel displaced upward into it finds air that is warmer and therefore denser than itself and sinks back. The smoke is released at 40 metres, well below the 200 metre base of the inversion, so it cannot rise through the layer and is confined to the part of the valley below that contour. The depth available to it is therefore about 160 metres, not the 400 metres of valley relief, and the mixing volume has been cut by more than half. That is the reason inversions are so damaging for air quality: the emissions are unchanged but the volume they are diluted into is not. The classic pattern of an inversion is a fumigation, in which the mixing height grows through the morning as the ground is heated from below, clearing the accumulated pollutant suddenly, and an emergency plan that assumes steady dispersion through the night will be wrong on exactly the worst night.

questions.explanation: The two rates describe one parcel before and after it reaches its dew point, and the difference between them is the reason rain falls at all. A rising unsaturated parcel cools at the dry rate, so the dew point is reached at a predictable height, and from that moment the release of latent heat reduces the rate of cooling to the moist one. A saturated parcel keeps rising only while it is warmer than the air around it, so the ascent continues until it meets air of its own temperature, and the level where that happens is the condensation level of any cloud it forms. That is why the rate at which a front's cloud deepens, and the height of the tops of the clouds in a frontal system, can both be read off from a single environmental lapse rate. The two figures are not alternatives to be averaged: a rising parcel passes through both regimes, and the altitude at which it changes from one to the other is fixed by its own humidity.

questions.explanation: The two distributions are the evidence for two different processes. An earthquake needs a sudden release of strain, which requires friction, and friction acts wherever two plates are locked together, so the shallow quakes spread along the whole length of a boundary. The arc is found where the slab has descended to about 100 km, since that is the depth at which water is released from the slab and the mantle wedge above it begins to melt. Setting 100 km equal to the run times the tangent of the dip gives a run of 173 km, above which the slab is at 57.7 km. Both figures come from the same geometry and both depend on the dip, which is why the dip has to be measured rather than assumed: a shallower slab puts the deep events further out and the arc closer in, and a steeper one does the reverse. The 100 km melting depth is a rule of thumb for a wet slab, and it moves for a hot one.

questions.explanation: The lithosphere is crust plus rigid upper mantle, and its thickness is set by the temperature of that mantle rather than by the thickness of the crust, which is why oceanic lithosphere is commonly taken to be about 100 km thick where it leaves a spreading ridge and thickens as it cools away from it. questions.explanation: The crust on one side of a ridge moves away at the half-rate, so the age at a distance from the axis is the distance divided by 3 centimetres a year, not by 6. Converting 5,400 km gives 5.4 times 10 to the eighth centimetres, and dividing by 3 gives 1.8 times 10 to the eighth years, which is 180 million years. The same relation applied nearer the axis gives 40 million years at 1,200 km and 90 million at 2,700 km, and those two are exactly half and a quarter of 180, which is the check that the age increases linearly with distance. The relation being inverted here is the one people get wrong: 6 centimetres a year is how fast the two plates separate, which is a property of the pair, while the age of any particular piece of crust is set by the speed of its own plate, and using 6 would halve every age. The oldest ocean floor found anywhere is close to 180 to 200 million years old, and this calculation reproduces that figure from a plausible half-rate.

questions.explanation: A column floats when the mass it displaces equals the mass it has, and thickening the crust adds mass while raising the surface removes an equal volume of mantle. Writing the balance with a root of depth r and a relief of h gives r times the density difference equal to h times the mantle density, so r equals 6 times 3,300 divided by 500, which is 39.6 km. The check is direct: 39.6 kilometres of root replacing mantle removes 39.6 times 500, or 19,800 kilograms per cubic metre of column, and the 6 km of relief removes 6 times 3,300, also 19,800. The new crustal thickness is the original 32 plus the root minus the relief, which is 65.6 km, and that is the figure a seismic survey would measure. The scaling is worth noting: 4 km of relief needs 26.4 km of root and 1 km needs 6.6, so the root is always about 6.6 times the relief, which is what makes very high mountains possible at all.

questions.explanation: The requirement is one of buoyancy, not of strength. Crust is less dense than the mantle beneath it, so a thicker column of crust is a column that has pushed more mantle out of the way than its extra mass justifies, and it will only stay where it is if the extra mass is balanced by the mass of the mantle it has displaced. That is the root, and its depth follows directly from the density contrast: with a contrast of 500 kilograms per cubic metre a root of 39.6 km is needed to support 6 km of relief. The arithmetic also shows why the height of mountains is limited. Each additional kilometre of relief requires about 6.6 km of root, and a root that grows without limit eventually meets mantle that is too hot to support the stress, so the process runs out of room. Flexure of the lithosphere offers an alternative support, and where the lithosphere is stronger it is used, which is why a load on a thick craton depresses the surface by a smaller fraction of itself than the Airy model predicts.

questions.explanation: Drainage density is the total length of channel divided by the area, so 128 divided by 64 is 2.00 kilometres of channel per square kilometre. The measure is a property of the landscape as a whole rather than of any one valley, and it says how efficiently the ground is organised into channels rather than how large the main river is. Two landscapes with identical total relief and identical annual rainfall can differ by a factor of ten in drainage density, and the difference is a difference in what resists erosion. Permafrost, dry sandy soils and consolidated glacial deposits all hold a low density because infiltration and storage are easy, while shale, thin soils over bedrock and steep humid catchments hold a high density. The definition also decides what is counted: a figure that includes only channels above a mapped threshold will be much smaller than one that includes every rill, so a drainage density is meaningless without the mapping convention that produced it.

A value of 1 would mean a straight channel, and every value above 1 records how much further the water travels than a straight line would take. This is not a trivial inefficiency: at a sinuosity of 1.67 the channel is 67% longer than the valley it occupies, so for the same discharge the gradient along the channel is 67% smaller and the flow is slower. Meandering is also self-maintaining, because the outer bank is eroded where the bend is tightest and the inner bank is built where the bend is widest, so the geometry that produces the meander is the geometry the meander preserves.

answer.exemplar: The return period is a rank, not a clock. A record of n years of annual peak flows is sorted from largest to smallest, and the flow in position m is assigned a return period of n plus one divided by m, so in a 20-year record the largest flood has a return period of 21, the second has 10.5, the third 7, and the smallest 1. That is the whole of the calculation, and everything that is often said about the number grows out of two separate mistakes. The first is treating the return period as an interval, so that a 10-year flood is assumed to be waiting for the decade to turn; nothing in the record supports that, because the order of the years carries no information about the order of future years, and a flood far larger than any in the record can arrive in any year of the next. The second is reading the number as a probability of not happening, which reverses it: a return period of 10 years is equivalent to a probability of about one in ten in any single year, so in a century the flood should be expected roughly ten times over, and its absence over that century would be the surprising outcome. The correct way to state the finding is in terms of the annual exceedance probability and of the risk over whatever period the decision actually covers, and to say how wide the estimate is, since a return period computed from a short record rests on a handful of observations and its confidence interval is wide.

questions.explanation: The calculation and the two misreadings have to be kept apart, because the number itself is a direct consequence of the record length and the rank of the flow in it. Everything that is claimed about the future comes from assumptions the calculation does not contain, which is why the risk over the period a decision actually covers is the figure to quote and why the width of the estimate matters as much as its size.
questions.hint: Start from the rank of the flow in the sorted record, then ask what that says about timing.
questions.learningObjective: explain how a return period is computed and correct the two standard misreadings

The time to peak is not the same quantity, because the hydrograph has to rise and fall, and a catchment of this size reaches its peak only after the last of the rain has fallen; the usual approximation puts the time to peak near one and a half times the concentration time, so about 38 minutes here. The second route writes it through the transmissivity, which is the conductivity times the saturated thickness, so 12 times 8 gives 96 square metres a day, and the discharge is the transmissivity times the gradient times the width, which is 96 times 0.02 times 625 and again gives 1200. The two forms are algebraically identical and both are in common use, the transmissivity form being the one that is normally reported for an aquifer because it folds the thickness into a single number. In other units the same flow is 0.01389 cubic metres a second, which is a useful reminder that the convenient daily unit conceals how small a groundwater flux is. The gradient is the head loss per unit distance, and it is the only term in the equation that a manager can change quickly, which is why pumping and drainage are the practical instruments.

questions.explanation: A catchment water budget is a statement of conservation, and it has to close: precipitation has to equal what leaves as evapotranspiration, what leaves as runoff and what is retained as a change in storage. Here 620 plus 250 plus 30 is exactly 900, so the four figures are mutually consistent and any of them could be computed from the other three. The runoff coefficient is the fraction of precipitation that leaves as runoff, so 250 over 900 is 0.278, and the same number comes out of one minus the evapotranspiration share of 0.689 minus the storage share of 0.033. The evapotranspiration share of 0.689 is the number that would move first in a discussion of land use, because it is the one term a change in vegetation or in soil can shift: a catchment with more forest returns more of its precipitation to the atmosphere and delivers less to the outlet, which is a change in the timing of the flow as well as in its amount. A budget that does not close is telling you that at least one of the measurements is wrong, and closing it is the first check on any new dataset.

questions.explanation: Texture classes are defined by the clay percentage first and only then by the balance between sand and silt, because clay controls the behaviour of a soil: its water retention, its cation exchange and its strength when wet all follow from the surface area the clay provides. With 30% clay the sample lies in the 27 to 35% band, which is the clay loam range, and within that band a soil becomes a sandy clay loam only when the sand fraction is low enough to leave the sandy class. The decisive step in any classification is to consult the triangle rather than to reason from the percentages, because the boundaries are drawn to keep the number of classes manageable and they are not intuitive. Two practical points follow. The classes are not equal intervals of anything, so a change of 5% in clay can move a sample across a boundary. And texture is only a coarse description: two soils of identical texture can differ completely in structure, and structure is what governs the rate at which water moves through the profile.

Converting the gravimetric water content to a volumetric one requires the bulk density, since water mass becomes volume only through the volume of soil that mass occupies, so 0.20 multiplied by 1.35 is 0.27, or 27% of the soil volume. The air porosity is therefore 49.1 minus 27, which is 22.1%, and the three numbers together, 27 plus 22.1 plus 51, sum to the whole volume. That decomposition is the useful one, because it shows that a soil at 20% gravimetric water is neither dry nor saturated: it holds water in roughly half its pores and air in the other half, which is the condition a plant root system needs. Compaction is what destroys the arrangement, and it destroys the large pores first, so a compacted soil can hold as much water in total while holding far less that a plant can extract.

questions.explanation: Available water is the water between field capacity and wilting point, so the contribution of each horizon is the difference of its two water contents multiplied by its thickness in millimetres. The top horizon gives 0.18 times 300, which is 54 mm; the middle gives 0.18 times 400, which is 72 mm; and the bottom gives 0.14 times 300, which is 42 mm. The total is 54 plus 72 plus 42, which is 168 mm. The same figure comes out of the profile totals, since the field capacities sum to 274 mm and the wilting points to 106 mm, and the difference is also 168. The profile is worth reading as a whole: the bottom horizon contributes the least per unit depth because its clay fraction is lowest and its water is held more tightly, and a soil whose available water is concentrated near the surface is more vulnerable to drought than one with the same total spread through the profile. That is why a subsoil clay horizon, even when it adds little to the total, changes how long the profile takes to dry out.

questions.explanation: Field capacity is the water content after drainage has removed the water that gravity will take, and the wilting point is the water content below which roots cannot extract water at all, so the difference between them is the only part of the soil's water that is both present and available. The two values on their own say very little: a sandy soil can have a high field capacity expressed as a fraction and a small gap, and a clay soil the reverse, which is why a clay soil holds more total water and a sandy soil gives it up more readily. The gap also carries information about the pore size distribution, since water held between the two states is held in the smaller pores and on the surfaces of the larger ones. What the gap does not include is water that moves by capillary action from a wetter part of the profile, which is why a crop growing on a subsoil can survive a surface that looks completely dry.

questions.explanation: Cation exchange capacity is a measure of the negative charge on clay and organic matter that can hold positively charged ions, and it is a property of the mineralogy rather than of the size distribution, which is why two soils of identical texture can differ by a factor of six. A high capacity means the exchange sites are numerous, so an addition of lime or fertiliser changes the concentration of the soil solution only slightly and the added nutrient stays in exchangeable form where a root can take it up; a low capacity means the same addition swings the solution concentration sharply, part of the nutrient is lost by leaching before it is taken up, and the soil has to be limed more often to hold its pH. questions.explanation: A humid profile is a set of transports, not a set of layers. Rain water percolating through the upper horizon dissolves and disperses clay, iron and aluminium and carries them down, which is eluviation, and that upper horizon is left pale and friable, often with a concentration of quartz sand and of resistant minerals. The material is redeposited where the percolating water slows, usually at the top of a less permeable horizon, which is illuviation, and the receiving horizon acquires the darker colour and the blocky or clay-enriched structure that comes from clay being rearranged. The pairing is diagnostic because the two horizons are complementary: a pale eluviated horizon with no clay-enriched horizon beneath it is unusual, and usually means the water is leaving the profile sideways rather than percolating through it. A change of land use or a drainage improvement can shift the boundary between the two, and monitoring that boundary is one of the few ways to see soil development over a human timescale.

questions.explanation: Texture governs the pore size distribution, and the size of the pores is what decides how much of the water a crop can get. A clay soil has a far larger total pore space than a sand, so it holds more water, but most of that water is in pores small enough or held tightly enough that roots cannot extract it: its available water capacity is high while its field capacity is much higher still. A sand holds little water, and what it holds is almost all available, so it dries out quickly and must be irrigated often in small amounts that the soil can absorb rather than lose. The consequence for management is not merely frequency but depth and rate. A clay soil is best irrigated less often, more deeply and more slowly, since a heavy application runs off a surface that has already reached field capacity, while a sand is best irrigated often and lightly, since a heavy application drains straight through. The same argument is why organic matter matters so much on a sand: it raises the available capacity, which is the term a sandy soil has least of.
questions.hint: Compare the available water capacity of the two, not the total pore space.

questions.explanation: A profile builds from the surface downwards, and each stage creates the conditions for the next. Organic residues have to arrive and weather before there is a dark, biologically active surface horizon, because that horizon is made of the residues themselves and of the aggregates they bind. Weathering then works on the parent material, which is the only source of the clay and the oxides that the later stages move, so nothing can be transported before it has been released. Eluviation follows, carrying that material down out of the horizons above, and illuviation follows the eluviation because the material has to be somewhere to be deposited. The last step is not a process but a description: the boundary between the two lower horizons stops moving once the supply and the removal have reached a balance, and the profile is then described as mature. Reading a profile in that order turns a colour photograph into a history, and it is also the reason a young soil on a recently disturbed surface has an A horizon and nothing else.

answer.exemplar: A point on a biome diagram is a summary of two annual averages, and the class it falls in is a prediction of the vegetation that will dominate there. The two axes matter for different reasons. Annual mean temperature sets the growing season, since a mean below freezing implies a season in which nothing photosynthesises, and it is also a proxy for the rate at which chemical processes proceed. Annual precipitation sets whether water is limiting, but only in combination with temperature, because the same rainfall supports forest in a cool place and scrub in a warm one, since the demand of the atmosphere rises with temperature. The boundaries on the diagram are drawn by joining points where the vegetation actually changes, so they mark real transitions and not merely the middle of the range of the plants concerned, and their shape is a consequence of the two-variable classification rather than a geometric necessity. The last point is the one that matters most for interpretation. The same annual mean temperature and the same annual precipitation can be produced by a mild, evenly watered climate and by one with a long dry season and a short intense wet one, and the vegetations will be entirely different even though the point plots in the same place. A third pair of facts can change the balance further: the depth of the soil, the time of the last disturbance, and the arrival of a fire or of grazing, each of which can hold a community in a state the climate alone would not predict.

questions.explanation: The question has three parts and the third is the one that catches people: the same two annual averages can be produced by very different seasonal distributions of rainfall, so the classification is a statement about averages rather than about the year a plant actually experiences. Reading the diagram therefore has to be paired with the monthly record, otherwise a monsoon climate and a Mediterranean one can plot in the same box.
questions.hint: Ask what the two axes stand for, why the boundaries fall where they do, and what the averages leave out.
questions.learningObjective: interpret a point on a biome diagram and the limits of the classification

questions.explanation: The budget has three terms and two of them are outputs. Gross production is the total fixed by photosynthesis at 2,200 grams, plant respiration of 1,100 is the cost of running the plants themselves, and net primary production is what is left for growth, which is 1,100. Soil and decomposition respiration of 900 then works on the litter that growth produced, and subtracting it gives a net ecosystem production of 200 grams per square metre a year. The sign is the point of the exercise: a positive net ecosystem production means the stand is accumulating carbon in its own biomass and its soils, and a young stand at this rate is a carbon sink, while the same measurements on a mature stand would normally give a figure near zero because the litter input and the decomposition loss balance. questions.explanation: A boundary drawn on a vegetation map is a convention, and like every boundary it is a choice about where to put the line through something that does not have one. The processes that separate the communities overlap, so at any given boundary there is a zone in which the two are mixed, and the width of that zone depends on the rate at which the controlling factor changes, which is why a boundary on a steep environmental gradient is narrow and one on a gentle gradient is wide. A second complication is disturbance: a single fire, a fence or a path can hold a community in place inside what is otherwise a different environment, and such outliers are the reason a vegetation map must be drawn at a scale appropriate to the survey rather than at the scale of the mechanism. The honest treatment is to map the transition as a band with a stated width, to record how the width was determined, and to keep the distinction between a mapped boundary and an observed one, since a mapped one is an estimate with an uncertainty attached.

The same figure comes out of the split between the outputs, since 7 divided by 42 is 16.7% of the loss is denitrification and the rest leaves in the product. A positive balance means the watershed is accumulating nitrogen, and only 26.7% of the inputs, that 12 from fixation, arrive from outside the system; the other three quarters are added by management, and the accumulation is a measure of that dependence. questions.explanation: Nitrogen saturation is the state in which a watershed can no longer take up additional nitrogen without exporting it, and the signature is exactly the one described. In the early years of rising application, each increment of fertiliser was largely taken up by crops, soil storage and microbial immobilisation, so the export rose only slowly. As the available storage and the biological demand are filled, an increasing share of each increment leaves by denitrification and by runoff, and the export curve flattens against a rising input. The two readings in the distractors both assume the surplus has been absorbed, and the third assumes a change in the flow without evidence, but the standard interpretation of a plateau in export against rising load is saturation. Its management consequence is direct: once the watershed is saturated, additional fertiliser buys almost no extra yield and simply raises the concentration in the water, so the profitable response is to stop adding and to start recovering the storage that has already been filled.

answer.exemplar: A carbon budget is an accounting identity, and an accounting identity settles a question of arithmetic and nothing else. Written for a landscape it has three terms: carbon fixed by photosynthesis, carbon returned by plant respiration, and carbon returned by the decomposition of litter and by the soil. The difference between the second and third terms and the first is the net balance, and a positive figure means the landscape is accumulating carbon in biomass and in soil while a negative figure means it is losing both. That much is not in dispute, and it is the reason a young forest that is growing reports a sink while a cleared one reports a source. What the budget does not settle is why the balance has the sign it has, because a positive figure can come from growth, from a change in the soil pool, or from a reduction in the rate at which carbon is being burnt, and those three require different responses. Nor does it settle for how long, since a sink sustained by regrowing forest is temporary by construction, and reporting a rate without a timescale invites the reader to treat it as permanent. The budget is also silent about where the carbon goes once it is fixed, and a large fraction never reaches the atmosphere at all, having passed through plants that were eaten or that died. A budget is therefore the place to start a discussion of carbon, not the end of one, and the useful practice is to publish the three terms separately so that a reader can see which of them is doing the work.

questions.explanation: The distinction the answer has to make is between the sign of the balance, which the arithmetic settles, and the cause of that sign, which it does not. Three terms enter the budget and any of them can move, so a net figure has to be published with its components and read together with the timescale over which it has been measured.
questions.hint: Separate what an accounting identity settles from what it leaves open, and watch the timescale.

answer.exemplar: The missing three quarters is not lost, it is accounted for, and the accounting is a water budget. Rainfall that reaches the ground either runs off, returns to the atmosphere by evaporation from the soil, by transpiration through vegetation, or by evaporation from the canopy and from interception, or is stored in the soil, in lakes and in the groundwater body, and storage is a transfer between one store and another rather than a loss. The terms are not fixed, and that is the reason the ratio varies between catchments and between years. The evaporative share depends on temperature and on the availability of water, so it is high in a warm year and low in a cool one with the same rainfall. The storage share depends on the geology, on the soil and on how the catchment has been drained, and a catchment with deep permeable rock can hold several years of water underground, which is why its ratio swings from year to year while a shallow, saturated catchment's does not. Vegetation changes the evaporative share directly, and a forested catchment typically returns more of its rainfall to the atmosphere than a cropped one on the same rainfall. The ratio is therefore a fingerprint of the whole water balance of a catchment, and it is a useful summary only alongside the observations of soil moisture and groundwater level that explain it.

questions.explanation: The ratio is a summary of a whole water balance rather than a property of the rainfall, and every term in that balance varies with climate, soils, geology and land use. That is the argument for treating a transfer of a measured ratio from one catchment to another as an assumption to be tested, rather than as a coefficient that can be applied.

Peak flood discharge changes too, but it does so through interception and through the roughness of the canopy, and the effect on the largest flood of the century is the smallest of all, because a big flood is governed by saturated soils and by the routing of the channel. Sediment yield falls, but it does so only once the canopy and the litter layer are established, which is several years. A useful discipline when planning such a programme is to order the candidate measurements by the product of how quickly they respond and how large a change they can carry, and to fund the one at the top of that list first.
